lessonTitle: Viral Structure and Replication: Genomes, Envelopes, the Replication Cycle and Influenza Variation

blocks.text: Every winter a vaccine tailored to last year's influenza strains is updated, yet roughly every few decades a strain emerges that almost nobody is immune to and spreads worldwide in months. Both facts come from the same virus; the difference lies in how its eight RNA segments change. To see why, we need to understand what a virus is built from and how it commandeers a cell.

blocks.markdown: Viruses are **obligate intracellular parasites**: they have no metabolism, no ribosomes and cannot replicate outside a host cell. A virion (virus particle) consists of a **nucleic acid genome**, either DNA or RNA, surrounded by a protein shell, the **capsid**, and in some viruses an outer lipid **envelope** studded with viral glycoproteins. Viruses are classified by genome type and presence of an envelope.

blocks.caption: Classification by genome (with examples)
rows: Replicate using host or viral DNA polymerase; herpesviruses are enveloped, adenovirus is not
Segmented; carries its own RNA polymerase
Poliovirus, rhinovirus, hepatitis C virus, SARS-CoV-2
Genome must be copied to mRNA by a viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase carried in the virion

blocks.title: Envelope
blocks.text: The envelope is a lipid bilayer derived from the host cell membrane (acquired when the virus buds out) that carries viral glycoproteins used for attachment and fusion. Enveloped viruses are inactivated easily by drying, detergents, soaps and alcohol; non-enveloped (naked) viruses are more stable and survive in the environment, in the gut and on surfaces.

blocks.caption: Enveloped versus non-enveloped viruses
rows: Fragile; destroyed by alcohol, soap, drying
Robust; resists alcohol, bile and drying

blocks.markdown: **The replication cycle.** Regardless of the virus, replication proceeds through a common sequence: (1) **attachment** of a viral surface protein to a specific receptor on the host cell (which determines tropism); (2) **penetration (entry)** by endocytosis or fusion of the envelope with the cell membrane; (3) **uncoating**, release of the genome from the capsid; (4) **genome replication and gene expression**: transcription of mRNA and translation of viral proteins, using host ribosomes, with the route depending on genome type (for example a negative-sense RNA virus must first make mRNA with its own polymerase); (5) **assembly** of new capsids and genomes; and (6) **release** by lysis of the cell or by budding through a membrane, which gives enveloped viruses their lipid envelope.

blocks.title: Sequencing the cycle
blocks.prompt: Place these events in order for an enveloped RNA virus: budding from the plasma membrane; fusion of the envelope with the cell membrane; translation of viral proteins; binding of the viral glycoprotein to its receptor; packaging of the genome into new capsids; release of the genome from the capsid.

steps.text: Attachment comes first: glycoprotein binds receptor.
Penetration: fusion of the envelope with the membrane, then uncoating: genome released.
Genome expression: translation of viral proteins and replication of the genome.
Assembly (packaging into capsids) then release by budding.

blocks.answer: Binding, fusion, uncoating, translation, packaging, budding.

blocks.markdown: **Effects on the host cell.** Outcomes include **cell death** (cytopathic effect, by lysis, shutdown of host synthesis or immune killing), **persistent or latent infection** (genome persists, as in herpesviruses) and occasionally **transformation** (uncontrolled growth). The tissue affected depends on receptor distribution.

**Influenza: drift and shift.** Influenza A is an enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA virus with a **genome in eight separate segments**. The surface glycoproteins **haemagglutinin (HA)**, which binds sialic acid receptors, and **neuraminidase (NA)**, which releases new virions, are the main antibody targets. **Antigenic drift** is the gradual accumulation of point mutations in the HA and NA genes, because the viral RNA polymerase lacks proofreading. Small changes let the virus partly escape existing immunity, causing yearly epidemics and the need for periodic vaccine updates. **Antigenic shift** is an abrupt major change that occurs when two different influenza A strains (for example human and avian or swine) infect the same cell and **reassort** their genome segments; a new combination of HA and NA appears to which the population has little immunity, and may cause a **pandemic**. Shift needs a segmented genome, whereas drift can happen to any RNA virus.

blocks.caption: Antigenic drift compared with antigenic shift
rows: Reassortment of genome segments between strains

blocks.caption: Plaque assay: each plaque is formed by one infectious particle (plaque-forming unit, PFU)

blocks.title: Counting infectious virus
blocks.prompt: A 10^-6 dilution of a virus stock is plated in a volume of 0.2 mL and gives 30 plaques. Calculate the titre.

steps.text: Denominator = 2 x 10^-7, so titre = 30 / (2 x 10^-7) = 1.5 x 10^8 PFU/mL.

blocks.title: Structure predicts behaviour
blocks.text: Genome type tells you how the virus makes mRNA, whether it needs its own polymerase, and what drugs act on it. The envelope predicts survival outside the body, the route of transmission, and how the virus leaves the cell.

blocks.title: Do not confuse drift with shift
blocks.text: Drift is mutation and is gradual; shift is reassortment and is abrupt. Only viruses with segmented genomes can undergo reassortment.

points: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites with a DNA or RNA genome, a capsid and sometimes a host-derived lipid envelope.
The replication cycle: attachment, penetration, uncoating, genome replication and expression, assembly, release.
Influenza drift is point mutation (epidemics); shift is segment reassortment (pandemics).

questions.stem: Which feature classifies a virus as enveloped?

options.text: A lipid bilayer derived from host membrane surrounding the capsid
A peptidoglycan layer
A DNA genome
A segmented genome

questions.correctOptionText: A lipid bilayer derived from host membrane surrounding the capsid

distractorRationale.c: Genome type does not define the envelope.
distractorRationale.d: Segmentation is a genome property, unrelated to the envelope.

questions.explanation: The envelope is a lipid bilayer acquired from the host cell, usually by budding. Genome type and segmentation are separate classification features.

questions.stem: A virus survives hand-rubbing with alcohol gel, is stable in the gut and is spread by the faecal-oral route. Which description fits best?

options.text: Non-enveloped virus
Enveloped virus
Retrovirus with a lipid envelope
A virus that needs no host cell

distractorRationale.b: Enveloped viruses are inactivated by alcohol and bile.
distractorRationale.d: All viruses need a host cell.

questions.explanation: Non-enveloped viruses lack a lipid envelope that alcohol or detergent can destroy. This stability explains faecal-oral spread and persistence on surfaces.

questions.stem: In which order do the stages of the viral replication cycle occur?

options.text: Attachment, penetration, uncoating, genome replication and expression, assembly, release
Uncoating, attachment, assembly, penetration, release, replication
Assembly, attachment, penetration, uncoating, replication, release
Penetration, release, attachment, uncoating, assembly, replication

questions.correctOptionText: Attachment, penetration, uncoating, genome replication and expression, assembly, release
questions.explanation: The virus must first attach and enter the cell, uncoat its genome, make its components, assemble new virions and then leave. Each stage depends on the previous one.

questions.stem: Why must a negative-sense single-stranded RNA virus carry an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase in the virion?

options.text: Its genome cannot be translated directly and host cells cannot copy RNA from an RNA template
Its genome is DNA and needs a reverse transcriptase
The capsid prevents access to host ribosomes
It must make the envelope using this enzyme

questions.correctOptionText: Its genome cannot be translated directly and host cells cannot copy RNA from an RNA template

distractorRationale.b: The genome is RNA, not DNA.
distractorRationale.c: Ribosomes translate mRNA after it is made.
distractorRationale.d: The enzyme copies RNA; the envelope comes from host membrane.

questions.explanation: A negative-sense genome is complementary to mRNA, so it cannot be translated until it is copied. Host cells lack RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, so the virus brings its own.

questions.stem: Which process produces a new influenza A haemagglutinin subtype that can cause a pandemic?

options.text: Reassortment of genome segments between two different strains in one cell
Point mutations accumulating in the haemagglutinin gene over a few seasons
Lysogenic integration of a prophage
Binding of antibody to neuraminidase

questions.correctOptionText: Reassortment of genome segments between two different strains in one cell

distractorRationale.d: Antibody binding does not generate a new subtype.

questions.explanation: Antigenic shift results when two strains co-infect a cell and swap genome segments, creating a novel HA or NA combination. Few people are immune, so a pandemic can follow.

questions.stem: A 10^-5 dilution of a virus preparation is plated in a volume of 0.1 mL and yields 45 plaques. Using titre = plaques / (dilution x volume in mL), calculate the titre in plaque-forming units per mL (PFU/mL). Give your answer in PFU/mL.
questions.explanation: Titre = 45 / (10^-5 x 0.1) = 45 / 10^-6 = 4.5 x 10^7 PFU/mL. Each plaque arises from one infectious particle, so the count measures infectious virus rather than total particles.

questions.stem: Influenza A has a genome of 8 segments. A cell is co-infected with two different parental strains, and each progeny virion receives each segment independently from either parent. Calculate the total number of distinct segment combinations possible (including the two parental genomes).
questions.explanation: Each of the 8 segments can come from one of 2 parents, so the number of combinations is 2^8 = 256, which includes the 2 parental genomes. This shows how reassortment can generate many novel genomes rapidly, some with new HA or NA.

questions.stem: Describe the stages of the viral replication cycle for an enveloped RNA virus that enters by membrane fusion and leaves by budding.
markingGuide: Attachment of viral glycoprotein to specific host receptor (determines tropism)
Penetration by fusion of envelope with membrane or endocytosis
Genome replication and translation of viral proteins using host machinery (and viral polymerase for RNA)
Release by budding, acquiring host-derived envelope
questions.explanation: The stages follow the needs of the virus: entry, production of components, assembly and exit. Budding explains where the envelope originates.

questions.stem: Classify viruses by genome type and presence of an envelope, and explain how the envelope influences survival outside the body and route of spread. Use one example of each category you mention.
markingGuide: Genome types: dsDNA (herpesvirus), ssDNA (parvovirus), dsRNA (rotavirus), positive-sense ssRNA (poliovirus), negative-sense ssRNA (influenza), retroviruses (HIV)
Envelope is host-derived lipid bilayer with glycoproteins
Enveloped viruses are fragile, inactivated by alcohol, soap and drying, so spread by close contact or droplets
Non-enveloped viruses are robust and spread by faecal-oral route or surfaces (such as norovirus)
Link to infection control: alcohol less reliable against non-enveloped viruses
questions.explanation: Genome type determines replication strategy, and the envelope determines stability and transmission. Together they predict much of a virus's behaviour.

questions.stem: Explain how antigenic drift differs from antigenic shift in influenza, and why shift is associated with pandemics while drift is associated with seasonal epidemics.
markingGuide: Drift: accumulation of point mutations in HA and NA genes due to error-prone RNA polymerase lacking proofreading
Shift: reassortment of the 8 genome segments when two strains infect the same cell
Drift gives small changes; partial existing immunity so seasonal epidemics and yearly vaccine updates
Shift gives novel HA/NA subtype to which the population has little or no immunity, so a pandemic can occur
Shift needs a segmented genome and co-infection, often involving animal strains
questions.explanation: The size of the antigenic change determines how much immunity remains. Small drift allows partial protection, whereas shift can create a virus against which almost no one is immune.
